title: Multi-Stage Builds
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of multi-stage builds.
Choose and interpret a suitable Docker example connected to multi-stage builds.
Predict an expected result and verify it using observable evidence in a controlled environment.

content.intro: This lesson covers Multi-Stage Builds. You will connect the named subtopics from the supplied Docker curriculum to a small, observable example. Work through the visual first, then use the example to form a prediction and check it against the actual behavior.
content.why_it_matters: Modern Docker builds use BuildKit capabilities for cache-aware build graphs, stage selection, secret mounts, and multi-platform output. A build cache is an optimization rather than a trust boundary; keep credentials out of image layers and validate the exact builder/driver and output behavior. Learning multi-stage builds helps you make deployment behavior explicit and repeatable instead of relying on a command that happened to work on one machine.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with the supplied example for multi-stage builds. Before running it, state what you expect to happen. Compare the real output with that prediction, then change one variable or setting in a disposable lab to test the boundary of the idea. If a command is not supported on your operating system or installed Docker version, consult the linked official reference and record the actual version rather than guessing.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Multi-Stage Builds
content_blocks.code:
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM nginx:alpine AS runtime
COPY --from=build /app/dist/ /usr/share/nginx/html/
content_blocks.expected_output: The final stage contains the web server and built static assets, not the Node build toolchain. The build assumes a project with package-lock.json and a dist output.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run `docker build -t codeleaf-multistage:local .` from a compatible frontend project folder.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming that a successful start means the application is ready.
common_mistakes.why: A container can start while its dependent service is unavailable or the application is failing after startup.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect health/status and logs; add a meaningful health check or retry strategy where appropriate.

common_mistakes.problem: Keeping required data only in the container writable layer.
common_mistakes.why: Replacing the container can discard that layer and its application state.
common_mistakes.fix: Select a named volume or an external storage system, then rehearse a restore.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a command without checking context, target, or permissions.
common_mistakes.why: Docker commands affect the active endpoint and can change host resources or publish services.
common_mistakes.fix: Check `docker context show`, use an isolated lab, make the smallest change, and verify the resulting state.
